fragments.text: AI provides expertise or experience that may otherwise be hard to come-by. It may be knowledge of many programming languages, knowing the word-for-word contents of a 500-page cybersecurity standard, or the best practices for configuring a firewall. This may be especially applicable to organizations that cannot afford top human talent.

Artificial intelligence (AI)1is rapidly changing our world and has significant potential to transform society and people’s lives. According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), remarkable surges in AI capabilities have led to a wide range of innovations including autonomous vehicles and Internet of Things devices in our homes.2It also holds substantial promise for improving the operations of government agencies. According to a supplement to the President’s fiscal year 2023 budget submission, agencies have requested $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI.3In addition, according to an executive order (EO) issued in December 2020, agencies are already using AI operationally to combat fraud, identify information security threats, and facilitate the review of large datasets, among other uses.4

Stanford, Udacity The importance of recent progress in Artificial Intelligence cannot be overstated. The field of AI has been around for more than 60 years, and it has had significant impact. AI is at the core of Google's search algorithms, Amazon's site design and Netflix's movie recommendations. But the advent of powerful computers paired with data set of unprecedented scale will be a game changer for society. In just the past few years, systems have been developed that rival or even outperform highly skilled people. Deep Mind's AlphaGo beats the world's best go players. In our own lab, we found that AI systems can diagnose skin cancer in images more accurately than some of the best board-certified dermatologists. I have long maintained that the Google self-driving car drives better than average drivers like myself. And the team is now operating these cars on public roads without the need of a safety driver. And Cresta, a start-up company, has shown that AI systems teamed with human specialists can double the efficacy of online sales teams. I believe that in the not-so-distant future, AI will be able to free us from repetitive work. AI systems will be able to watch human experts at work, and gradually acquire the skills we bring to bear in our daily work. As this happens, more and more repetitive work will be done by the machines, freeing us up to pursue more creative work.

As satellites become more capable, major U.S. space stakeholders must integrate artificial intelligence (AI) to preserve operational advantage. In 2020, Russia demonstrated an ability to closely shadow and subsequently test space-based weapons in the vicinity of U.S. satellites. 7 In 2022, China—using its Shijian-class satellites—demonstrated an ability to tow other satellites out of their mission orbits. 8 These activities highlight an emerging threat: the ability of adversaries to exploit norms of behavior in space to gain first-mover advantage. Denying that advantage—through resilient, responsive systems—is central to deterrence in space. AI can help U.S. space forces avoid operational surprise in orbit. While AI has already transformed other space functions—such as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, two functions in particular stand to gain significant maturity: space domain awareness (SDA) and orbital warfare. These functions are critical to space control, and methodical application of AI to these areas would accelerate tactical decision-making, enhance satellite survivability, and increase orbital responsiveness. This paper examines how AI can augment SDA and orbital warfare capabilities, and outlines the policy recommendations needed to responsibly field such tools in future satellite architectures.

dos capacidades principales. En primer lugar, debido a su dependencia de las redes neuronales artificiales, requieren un cálculo paralelo masivo de unidades muy simples: las neuronas artificiales. En segundo lugar, debido a la enorme cantidad de datos utilizados durante la fase de entrenamiento, requieren una transferencia de datos muy rápida entre los recursos de almacenamiento y computación. Estas dos capacidades críticas no están presentes en las instalaciones HPC tradicionales, lo que las hace inadecuadas para implementar modelos de IA. En la actualidad, la principal infraestructura de apoyo a la I+D en IA se basa en las denominadas unidades de procesamiento gráfico o GPU. Las GPU, diseñadas originalmente para satisfacer las limitaciones en tiempo real de las tareas gráficas, como las animaciones visuales, están especialmente concebidas para realizar de forma masiva cálculos sencillos en paralelo. La falta de instalaciones computacionales basadas en GPUs o equipos computacionales similares es actualmente una de las principales debilidades
